title: Timed Practice
content_html:
Exam conditions

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — Classical Civilisation papers allocate approximately 1 minute per mark. An 8-mark essay should take no more than 8 minutes; a 10-mark question no more than 10. Time yourself accordingly.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Set an 8-minute timer and attempt this question cold: “How does Homer use the Cyclops episode to explore ideas about civilised and uncivilised behaviour?” Write by hand, no notes. Use the source-based argument scaffold: make a claim (the Cyclops represents the opposite of civilised Greek values), cite a specific literary detail (he eats his guests rather than hosting them — a direct inversion of xenia), add a material evidence parallel where you can (the contrast with the well-ordered Mycenaean megaron as a space for feasting and gift exchange), present an alternative view (the Cyclops is also portrayed with a degree of pathos — he prays to Poseidon, his own father — which complicates a simple monster reading), then reach a judgement. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it: did you make a claim, name a source, engage with an alternative, and conclude?

Example 2

Work through a 10-mark extended response under timed conditions: “How important was the concept of kleos in shaping the behaviour of Homeric heroes?” Allocate roughly 2 minutes to plan your argument scaffold before you write: define kleos (glory through great deeds, preserved in song); cite Odysseus’s behaviour (revealing his name to the Cyclops at the cost of Poseidon’s wrath — kleos overrides caution); the homecoming (the bow contest as public proof of identity and heroic status); the alternative view (Odysseus frequently uses disguise and deception, suggesting kleos is balanced against practical survival); your conclusion (kleos is the primary driver but Odysseus is unique among Homeric heroes in subordinating it when necessary). Write your answer in the remaining 8 minutes, then stop regardless of whether you have finished. Record which parts of the scaffold you reached — if you ran out before covering the counterargument, practise planning speed in the next session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per topic per week — usually a single question at first, building to full sections and then full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace. For the 8- and 10-mark extended responses specifically, practise the argument scaffold (claim → named literary evidence → named material evidence → alternative view → judgement) until it becomes automatic before the exam.

Quick Reference
Paper time + ~30 min marking

Build-up schedule

  1. One question, timed
  2. One section, timed
  3. Half a paper, timed
  4. Full paper, timed
  5. Full paper, exam conditions
  6. Mock week, all papers
